turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I do hope you're not suggesting that you're some sort of aristocrat, Mr. Worthing. I must say, I'm not entirely convinced of your credentials.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I must confess, Lady Bracknell, that my family's history is a bit... complicated. My mother was a widow, and I'm not entirely certain about my father's background.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am not surprised. The only thing that would have astonished me, Jack, is if your family's history were not complicated.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I'll not be lectured on my family's history by you, Lady Bracknell. I'm perfectly aware of the scandals that surround me, and I'm not ashamed of them.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I'm astonished, Jack, that you would think it necessary to defend my daughter's family history. I suppose it's only to be expected from someone who's never had the benefit of a proper education.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I didn't mean to imply that, Lady Bracknell. I was simply trying to explain myself, so that Gwendolen might understand why I'm not, ah, quite as well-connected as some other gentlemen she's met.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I fail to see how your rather vague explanation, Mr. Worthing, sheds any light on your suitability as a husband for my daughter. Tell me, have you any family, any connections that might recommend you to me?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I do hope, Mother, that you're not suggesting I'm not suitable for Jack because of our engagement!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am not at all satisfied with your answers, Mr. Worthing. You seem to be hiding something from me.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, I am not hiding anything from you. I am simply a humble young man who is not accustomed to being questioned in such a manner.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I do not appreciate this tone, Mr. Worthing. A gentleman such as yourself should be grateful for the opportunity to make a good impression, rather than growing defensive.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I didn't mean to be defensive, Lady Bracknell. It's just that this conversation is making me a bit anxious.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Anxiety, I suppose, is a natural consequence of being questioned by a member of the aristocracy. Pray tell, Mr. Worthing, do you have any explanation for the lack of stability in your past?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I'm not quite sure how to explain it, Lady Bracknell. I've been trying to make amends for my past mistakes, and I'm hoping that my engagement to Miss Gwendolen is a good start in that regard.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I do hope you're not implying that my engagement to Jack is anything less than a perfect match, Mother. I'm perfectly capable of making my own decisions about my life.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I wouldn't dream of implying otherwise, Lady Bracknell. I'm sure Miss Gwendolen is more than capable of making her own decisions, and I'm grateful for her trust in me.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am not entirely convinced by your responses, Mr. Worthing. You seem to be evading the issue at hand.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, I am not evading the issue. I am simply trying to provide the most accurate information, as I am not quite sure how to answer some of these questions.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Really, Mr. Worthing, I must say I am growing weary of your evasions. Can you not provide a straightforward answer to a simple question?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't know what you'd like me to say, Lady Bracknell. I've tried to answer your questions as honestly as I can.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
